Article Title: In Kentucky, Jennifer Lawrence grew up on a family farm with horses, a butterfly garden and an animal rescue programme that led to puppy and kitten adoptions
Article Text:
Image: Left/StyleBlueprint/Right/Rex

How Henry County mud inspired Jennifer Lawrence's family farm, Camp Hi-Ho

Camp Hi-Ho activities in Simpsonville: Horses, archery, kayaks and more

Karen believes that education and advocacy play vital roles in advancing animal rescue and welfare (Image: StyleBlueprint)

How stray dogs and cats led to a Puppy Barn and Friday adoptions

Lawrence Family Foundation in Louisville and fundraising

Karen Lawrence's adventurous spirit: How she used to raise money for charity

Long before red carpets and golden statuettes, the Lawrence family had mud on their boots and a deep love of animals. Behind actress Jennifer Lawrence stands a Kentucky story that begins on a family farm, grows into a children's summer camp with horses and a butterfly garden, and expands into an animal rescue effort that changes lives. Karen Lawrence turned muddy summer afternoons and stray visitors into lasting community programmes, and this article follows that journey through the farm origins, the camp activities, the rescue work, the charitable foundation and the adventurous spirit that binds this close-knit Louisville family together.According to StyleBlueprint, the story starts with Karen Lawrence, a lifelong Louisvillian and University of Louisville alumna. After college, she noticed that families lacked after-school options, so she brought gymnastics classes into schools during the late 1970s and early 1980s. Later she ran camps at churches, where the local fire department hosed the children down on Fridays. Karen noticed the children preferred playing in the mud to almost anything else. That observation sent her thinking about the family farm in Henry County, which had plenty of mud.Friends became counsellors, the camp later moved to Simpsonville, and it was eventually sold to her child Blaine as Jennifer's career grew busier.Today Camp Hi-Ho is run by Blaine, and Karen praises the wonderful job done there. There’s arts and crafts, horses, archery, a lake, fishing, kayaks, paddle boats and a fort. Children can also relax in Hammock City, a corner of the camp where hammocks hang from trees and campers can read or simply daydream all day. Alongside these outdoor adventures sit a butterfly garden and a vegetable garden, giving young visitors a gentle introduction to nature and growing things. Karen describes the offering as something for everyone. For parents searching for a Kentucky summer camp that mixes horses, creativity, water play and quiet time, this combination shows how much variety the camp offers to children with many different interests.The animal rescue side of the story began almost by accident. As Karen told StyleBlueprint, food cooked at camp attracted stray dogs and cats, and she and her friends began taking the animals home on weekends so they would not go hungry. She spent thousands of dollars on neutering and vaccinations and nearly shut the effort down until the veterinarian, Dr Oliver of Lyndon Animal Hospital, offered his services. Rescued animals now stay in the Puppy Barn at camp, where campers learn how to care for them and may even take one home for a night. Adoptions of puppies and kittens take place on Fridays. The profile notes that advocacy and education matter greatly to Karen when it comes to animal rescue.Giving back is a family value, Karen explained to StyleBlueprint, and Jennifer's fame gave the Lawrence Family Foundation a bigger platform to raise money. The foundation tries to keep its fundraising in Louisville and supports basically anything related to children. One example is starting an arts programme for children in the West End who lack the opportunities available in the East End. The foundation also works with hospitals and with the Cancer Alliance Camp for children who have cancer. Each year it hosts a major fundraiser at Churchill Downs called Awards in the Arts, with cocktails, dinner and artists performing or singing. Karen also serves on the boards of the Louisville Orchestra and the Kentucky Film Commission, according to the profile.Karen Lawrence's generosity comes with a sense of adventure. She has jumped out of an aeroplane to raise money and scaled down the side of the Marriott Hotel building in downtown Louisville wearing a red cape while her grandchildren watched from below. At the time, she planned to perform as an amateur comedian at the Gilda's Club fundraiser, and she named Lucille Ball and Gilda Radner as her comedic idols. Her philosophy is simple, she will do anything at least once, including eating beetle larvae in Peru. Her advice to others is to live meaningfully and leave the world a better place than you found it. She also enjoys golf, tennis and adventurous travel, including a golf trip to Ireland the year before the interview.
Article Summary: Karen Lawrence started Camp Hi-Ho on her family farm in Henry County, Kentucky. Food cooked at camp attracted stray dogs and cats, and she and her friends began taking the animals home. Rescued animals now stay in the Puppy Barn at camp, where campers learn how to care for them and may even take one home for a night. Adoptions of puppies and kittens take place on Fridays.

Article Title: In 1929, Berlin’s planned birthday gift to Albert Einstein fell through; he built his own Caputh summer house, which became a meeting place for scientists, artists and thinkers
Article Text:
Representative Image of Albert Einstein’s peaceful Caputh summer house surrounded by nature ( AI Generrated Image)

Why Berlin’s birthday gift fell through, and how Einstein built his Caputh summer house

Einstein’s Caputh guestbook: Tagore, Max von Laue and other visitors

What happened to Einstein’s house after he left Germany?

Albert Einstein turned 50 on 14 March 1929, and Berlin planned to mark the occasion by providing him with a country house. The proposed gift fell through after difficulties over the properties offered and became the subject of public controversy. Einstein subsequently secured a site in Caputh, near Potsdam, and financed the construction of a timber summer house designed by architect Konrad Wachsmann. The retreat became a place where he could read, think, sail and welcome friends away from the demands of public life. Einstein spent much of the year there between 1929 and 1932, and a guestbook associated with the house offers a glimpse of some of its visitors. Today, the property remains connected to his life and work, as well as to the political circumstances that forced him to leave Germany.The plan for a house originated with Berlin mayor Gustav Böss, who wanted to honour Einstein on his 50th birthday. However, the original property under consideration had tenants, whom Einstein did not want evicted. Other proposals followed, but the city did not provide him with a completed house.The dispute attracted press attention and became entangled in political arguments in Berlin, including antisemitic remarks. Elsa Einstein learned of a possible site in Caputh through their neighbours, Adolf and Elsbeth Stern. Adolf Stern had offered land from his property, and the proposed gift ultimately led Einstein to pursue a summer house there. Accounts of the property’s history indicate that the land-register arrangements involved Einstein’s stepdaughters, Ilse and Margot, so the transaction should not be described simply as Einstein personally registering the land in his own name.Elsa learned of a possible site in Caputh through friends who offered part of their property. Einstein chose the location and decided to proceed with the house, which was designed by the young architect Konrad Wachsmann. Einstein financed the construction himself. The building permit was applied for on 12 May 1929 and approved in June. The house was completed in time for the family to move in during September 1929.The house was built primarily of wood and designed as a relatively simple summer retreat rather than a grand residence. Konrad Wachsmann, a young architect at the time, was responsible for its design. The house provided Einstein with a quiet place away from public demands, with the surrounding landscape and nearby Havel lakes offering opportunities for walks and sailing. The house itself was not the birthday present Berlin had intended to provide. Einstein received a sailing boat named Tümmler for his 50th birthday, which he used on the nearby lakes.Einstein welcomed visitors from scientific, literary and cultural circles, and the family’s guestbook preserves a partial record of these encounters. The neighbouring Sterns gave the book to the family as a housewarming gift, and Einstein jokingly instructed guests to write in verse rather than ordinary prose.Among the figures associated with Einstein’s Caputh circle was the Indian poet and philosopher Rabindranath Tagore. The painter Hermann Struck illustrated a page of the guestbook in autumn 1931, and the page also bears the signature of Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann. Other visitors to Caputh included conductor Erich Kleiber and violinist Ruggiero Ricci, although their names should not be presented as guestbook entries unless independently verified. The original guestbook is held by the Leo Baeck Institute in New York.Einstein and Elsa left Caputh for the United States in December 1932. As the Nazi regime consolidated power, Einstein did not return to Germany. The house was searched on 20 March 1933. Accounts of its confiscation give different dates in 1935. Its subsequent history reflected the political upheavals of the period and changing decisions about how the property should be used and maintained. The East German Academy of Sciences restored the house in 1978–79, around the centenary of Einstein’s birth, and used it as a guest house and memorial. After German reunification, the Einstein Forum assumed administrative responsibility for the property in 1993. A later renovation, supported by the German federal government and the Cornelsen Culture Foundation, prepared the house for the Einstein Year in 2005. The Hebrew University of Jerusalem is the property’s majority owner.Today, Einstein’s summer house remains a place for historical reflection and intellectual exchange. Public access and guided tours depend on current arrangements, so visitors should confirm details with the Einstein Forum or the property’s administrator before travelling to Caputh. The house offers a glimpse of Einstein’s life away from public duties, but its history also reflects the antisemitic persecution that forced him to leave Germany and the later efforts to preserve the property as part of his legacy.
Article Summary: Einstein turned 50 on 14 March 1929, and Berlin planned to give him a country house. The proposed gift fell through after difficulties over the properties offered. Einstein secured a site in Caputh, near Potsdam, and financed the construction of a timber summer house designed by architect Konrad Wachsmann. The retreat became a place where he could read, think and sail.

Article Title: A rare Canadian computer was forgotten in an Edmonton barn for decades; its first known unboxing came nearly 45 years after it was built
Article Text:
Image Credit: Carleton University

Importance of the rare Canadian computer discovery in an Edmonton barn

What made AES Data an important name in Canadian computing

How much is known about the Alphaplus 12 today

A forgotten machine returns to Canada's computing history

A rare Canadian-built computer that spent decades forgotten in a rural barn near Edmonton is preparing for a unique second chapter. The AES Alphaplus 12, believed to have been built around 1981, had resurfaced in its original shipping box and was taken to Carleton University in Ottawa for a scheduled public unboxing. The machine has attracted attention because so little documentation exists about this particular model, leaving its internal components and configuration uncertain. Its discovery offered a rare opportunity to examine a little-known part of Canada's early computing history.The rediscovery of the AES Alphaplus 12 is significant not simply because an old machine survived for decades, but because so little is known about the exact model. According to Carleton University's School of Computer Science, the computer remained untouched after its time at the Northern Alberta Institute of Technology (NAIT) before being forgotten in a rural Edmonton barn.The university's announcement, published on 2 September 2026, described the machine as a rare example of Canadian computing heritage. The 2 October unboxing event was scheduled to give specialists an opportunity to identify and assess the machine, and also to establish what can be learned from the surviving hardware.The university also noted that the machine was sealed in its dusty shipping box. That condition made the discovery particularly intriguing, as its contents had not yet been examined in the context of the planned public unboxing.The story of the Alphaplus 12 is closely connected to the development of electronic word processing in Canada. Carleton University's background article identifies Montreal-based AES Data Ltd. as the company behind the machine and traces its design lineage to the earlier AES-90.The AES-90 was an important development because it used a screen to display and edit text electronically. According to Carleton, it introduced capabilities such as automatic line wrapping, text justification and numerical alignment at a time when these functions were far from standard. In 1972, the press described the machine as an electronic editor, reflecting how different it was from conventional typing equipment.By 1978, AES was competing directly with IBM as Canada's largest word-processing supplier, according to the university's account. The company was acquired by Ottawa's Kinburn Technology Corporation in 1987, creating a further connection between its history and the city where the newly recovered machine was taken.Despite AES Data's importance in the word-processing industry, information about the Alphaplus 12 itself remains remarkably scarce. Carleton's School of Computer Science reported finding only 2 pieces of documentation relating specifically to the model. A listing in a British museum archive and a brief reference in a Canadian trade magazine from 1981.Even Ingenium, Canada's national science and technology museum, has early AES word processors and software in its collection but no record of this particular model, the university reported. That gap made the recovered machine especially valuable to researchers trying to establish a clearer picture of the country's computing history.A separate entry in the Time-Line Computer Archive provides some context about the wider Alphaplus family. Its listing for the AES Alphaplus 14 describes a word processor built in the early 1980s by the Montreal-based company. The archive explains that the machine was designed for word processing rather than as a general-purpose computer and features a printer built into the monitor.However, the archive documents the Alphaplus 14, not the recovered Alphaplus 12. Its description therefore offers background on related equipment, rather than proof of the exact features or configuration of the barn discovery.The unboxing at Carleton University took place on 2nd October at 2 pm in room 4155 of the Herzberg Building where a livestream was also planned, according to the university's announcement on 18 September 2026.Carleton's announcement places the discovery within a wider pattern of vintage-computing finds. The university's background article recalls the appearance of roughly 2,200 NABU computers from a barn in Massachusetts in 2023. Those machines had their own Canadian connection, having been developed by the Ottawa-based NABU Network in the early 1980s. It also describes the discovery of two Q1 microcomputers beneath boxes at Kingston University in London.The Alphaplus 12 is a smaller discovery in scale, but its limited documentation made it a unique find in its own right. Its journey from an educational institution in Alberta to decades of obscurity in a barn had left important details about the machine unresolved.
Article Summary: AES Alphaplus 12, believed to have been built around 1981, resurfaced in its original shipping box and was taken to Carleton University in Ottawa for a scheduled public unboxing. The machine has attracted attention because so little documentation exists about this particular model, leaving its internal components and configuration uncertain.

Article Title: Utah approved blasting 100-foot canyon cliffs to widen a 5.3-mile road for oil trucks; after two earlier plans failed, a new federal lawsuit says 47 historic sites and 19th-century inscriptions are at
Article Text:
(Photo courtesy: Center for Bioloical Diversity)

Why the canyon’s rock inscriptions are at risk

Photo courtesy: Reuters

Road project could increase oil-truck traffic

Conservation groups challenge federal approval

An earlier challenge to the proposed oil route

A plan to widen and pave a road through a historic canyon in the US state of Utah has triggered a new federal lawsuit, with conservation groups warning that the project could destroy cliff walls bearing 19th-century inscriptions and damage a landscape known for its Native American rock art.The lawsuit challenges the US Bureau of Land Management’s approval of a project to widen, straighten and pave the existing Gate Canyon Road in eastern Utah. The proposed work would involve blasting sections of canyon walls, some measuring around 100 feet (30 metres) high, to accommodate increased traffic, including trucks travelling to oil fields.According to a Reuters report, conservation groups filed the lawsuit this week, arguing that the project threatens historic sites and wildlife habitats in the area. The complaint was filed on October 6 in the US District Court for the District of Utah.The lawsuit identifies at least 47 historic sites along or near the existing road, including inscriptions made by Black American soldiers who served in the US Army’s Buffalo Soldiers regiments during the 19th century. European pioneers and freighters also left their names on the canyon walls, with some inscriptions made using axle grease.The complaint states that 43 of the 47 historic sites are considered eligible for inclusion on the National Register of Historic Places, the official list of historic properties recognised for their significance in American history.The plaintiffs argue that blasting and realigning the road could destroy these features, which offer a record of people who travelled through the region and helped build its existing route.The concerns extend beyond the inscriptions. Gate Canyon connects to Nine Mile Canyon, an area recognised for its concentration of Native American rock art and archaeological remains. The US Bureau of Land Management describes Nine Mile Canyon as the “world’s longest art gallery”.According to Reuters, Nine Mile Canyon stretches for approximately 46 miles (74 km) and contains more than 1,000 rock-art sites with over 10,000 images, some dating to prehistoric times.The Gate Canyon project was proposed by Duchesne County to replace a winding dirt track with a paved road. The improved route would provide an alternative truck corridor to the Uinta Basin oil fields.However, the conservation groups contend that the road could increase traffic through Gate Canyon and the adjoining Nine Mile Canyon region, placing its archaeological, scenic and environmental features under greater pressure.The lawsuit also raises concerns about wildlife, including the threatened Mexican spotted owl, whose habitat could be affected by the construction and associated changes to the area.In its complaint, the groups argue that the Bureau of Land Management approved the project in April 2026 without adequately assessing its foreseeable effects on cultural resources, historic sites, scenery and wildlife. They also allege that the agency did not provide the public with an opportunity to review and comment on the proposal before approving it.The claims are allegations made by the plaintiffs and have not been established by a court.The lawsuit was brought by the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and the Center for Biological Diversity. They are asking the court to set aside the federal approval of the project.The complaint alleges violations of several federal laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Endangered Species Act and the Federal Land Policy and Management Act. These laws include requirements relating to environmental impacts, historic preservation and the management of public lands.The complaint further argues that the agency failed to consult the US Fish and Wildlife Service about the project's foreseeable effects on threatened and endangered species.The US Department of the Interior, which oversees the Bureau of Land Management, told Reuters it had no comment because litigation was pending.The dispute follows a separate legal challenge announced in June 2026 by the Center for Biological Diversity over the proposed road development and its potential effects on Nine Mile Canyon.In a June 15 press release, the organisation described the proposed route as an oil highway that could threaten the canyon’s cultural and natural heritage. That announcement highlighted the broader conservation concerns surrounding increased oil-related traffic through the region.The latest lawsuit focuses on the Bureau of Land Management’s April approval of the Gate Canyon project and alleges that the decision failed to meet federal legal requirements.The case now places the proposed road improvements under judicial scrutiny, with conservation groups seeking to prevent the destruction of historic and environmental features before construction proceeds.
Article Summary: The lawsuit challenges the US Bureau of Land Management’s approval of a project to widen, straighten and pave the existing Gate Canyon Road in eastern Utah. The proposed work would involve blasting sections of canyon walls, some measuring around 100 feet (30 metres) high, to accommodate increased traffic. Conservation groups argue that the project threatens historic sites and wildlife habitats in the area.

Article Title: An Arkansas family treated the same fence as its property line for nearly six decades; after new neighbours removed fencing and trees, an appeals court upheld $12,000 in treble damages and an order to
Article Text:
The fence became more than just a fence

Tree removal resulted in $12,000 damages

The fence must be rebuilt

A fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties, after a dispute over trees and fencing reached the state Court of Appeals. The ruling in Floyd v. Bowlin-Lemon, reported by Justia, Leagle and Case Law Wire, affirmed the Bowlins’ boundary claim, a $12,000 treble-damages award and an order requiring the neighbouring owners to rebuild the fence. The case involved adjoining properties in Crawford County and centred on a fence line that the Bowlin family had treated as its southern boundary for decades. According to the Arkansas Court of Appeals, Joy Bowlin-Lemon’s family acquired the property in 1967. The family was shown the existing fence lines when it purchased the land and subsequently used those fences as practical boundaries. The property was used for livestock, including cattle and horses, while the family also maintained the land up to the fence by brush hogging and cutting hay.That arrangement remained unchallenged for decades. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property.The court record says portions of the longstanding fence were removed beginning in 2017, with the fence eventually torn down. Trees in the disputed area were also cut down. The Bowlins eventually filed a lawsuit in 2023, alleging trespass and destruction of their fencing and trees. A Crawford County Circuit Court trial followed in October 2024.The central legal question was whether years of treating the fence as the boundary could establish a legally recognised boundary even if the fence did not precisely match the surveyed property line. The appeals court said yes.Under Arkansas law, a boundary by acquiescence can arise when neighbouring landowners tacitly accept a particular line as the dividing boundary for a long period. The court noted that an express agreement is not required, nor does there need to have been an earlier dispute over the property line.In this case, the decades of maintenance and use along the fence, combined with the absence of objections from neighbouring owners, provided sufficient evidence for the lower court’s decision. The court also noted that the southern fence extended roughly 30 to 40 feet beyond the surveyed property line. Despite that discrepancy, the long-established conduct surrounding the fence supported its recognition as the boundary.The dispute also became costly for the Floyds. The circuit court determined that the trees removed from the disputed area were worth $4,000. The Arkansas Court of Appeals upheld that valuation, finding that testimony about the number and type of trees, photographs of the property and evidence of the clearing provided enough support.The court also upheld treble damages, bringing the total award to $12,000. Arkansas law allows treble damages when someone cuts, destroys or removes trees belonging to another person. The appeals court found enough evidence to support the finding that the tree removal was intentional or, at minimum, sufficiently reckless or negligent to trigger the statute. Among the evidence considered was the presence of no-trespassing signs along the fence and Ty Floyd’s admission that he removed trees and portions of the fencing.The lower court also ordered the Floyds to rebuild fencing along the eastern and southern boundaries. The appeals court left that order intact. It noted that Ty Floyd had indicated during the trial that he was willing to rebuild the fence, while his attorney did not object when the Bowlins requested the injunction.That meant the Floyds could not later challenge the fence-rebuilding requirement on appeal. There was, however, one issue the appeals court sent back to the circuit court. The original judgment did not contain a sufficiently precise legal description of the boundary. The appeals court therefore remanded the case for the limited purpose of adding a specific description that would allow the established boundary to be identified directly from the judgment.The decision underscores how decades of conduct can matter in property disputes. A fence may begin as a practical marker, but when generations of adjoining owners consistently treat it as the dividing line, that conduct can ultimately carry legal weight, even when a later survey points somewhere else.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments box below.
Article Summary: Fence that had been treated as a property boundary since 1967 has been upheld as the dividing line between two Arkansas properties. The dispute emerged after Ty Floyd, Kristy Floyd and Cottage Creations LLC acquired the neighbouring property. The Bowlin family had treated the fence line as its southern boundary for decades.

Article Title: ‘The Orange Plague’: Why a golden, naked Trump is sitting on another man
Article Text:
File photo: Visitors looks at a scupture titled "The Orange Plague" by Danish artist Jens Galschiot

What does the statue symbolise?

Why is Trump depicted naked?

Why has the statue been installed at the European Parliament?

Where else has ‘The Orange Plague’ been displayed?

A 2.6-metre-tall statue of US president Donald Trump, naked and coated in 23-karat gold leaf, has been installed inside the European parliament in Strasbourg, France.Titled ‘The Orange Plague’, the sculpture by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt depicts Trump sitting on the shoulders of a frail, smaller man, with his thighs and sagging belly wrapped around the man’s head. Trump holds a golf club in one hand and the scales of justice in the other. The work is also known as the “King of Injustice”.The sculpture is a satirical critique of what Galschiøt sees as Trump’s threats to the environment, international cooperation and the rules-based world order. The artist has said the US president is destroying the causes and institutions he believes in, including efforts to tackle climate change. The work also questions how political power is exercised and how its consequences are borne by those with less power.The smaller man beneath Trump represents the burden imposed by the powerful on the less powerful.A plaque at the base of the sculpture captures the imbalance through the words: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except step down from his back.”The imagery suggests a leader who claims to help others while continuing to place the weight of his power and decisions on them.The golf club and scales of justice add to the political satire, juxtaposing Trump’s personal image with the idea of justice. Its gold finish is also a deliberate choice: Galschiøt has pointed to Trump’s fondness for gold, saying he believes the president might even like the sculpture.Galschiøt has said the sculpture draws inspiration from Danish author Hans Christian Andersen’s fairy tale ‘The Emperor’s New Clothes’, in which a vain emperor parades through his city naked while those around him pretend he is wearing magnificent clothes.This is also not the first Trump sculpture to depict Trump naked based on a correlation with the fairy tale, a previous series of statues displayed across the US by an artist collective was also titled, ‘The Emperor Has No Balls’.By depicting Trump naked, Galschiøt seeks to ridicule the president and strip away the image of authority surrounding him. “Dictators don’t like you laughing at them,” the artist said, explaining the thinking behind the work.Galschiøt is known for provocative political art. His best-known works include the Pillar of Shame, a memorial to victims of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre that was controversially removed from a Hong Kong university in 2021. He has drawn a parallel between the two works, saying both concern the relationship between the powerful and the powerless.The exhibition was sponsored by Danish politician Per Clausen, a member of the European parliament’s left-wing group, The Left. Members of the European Parliament are entitled to sponsor cultural events and exhibitions on parliamentary premises, subject to approval by officials. The sculpture’s installation therefore does not amount to an official endorsement of its message by the European Union.Clausen said he wanted to encourage debate about how power is used around the world and how Europe can protect its interests without becoming dependent on Trump. He defended the exhibition as an opportunity to display work that not everyone might agree with.Galschiøt, who had feared the application would be rejected, viewed the approval as an opportunity to bring criticism of Trump into the European Parliament. He said many Europeans regard the US president’s conduct as a serious problem, even if they recognise that he is the leader of an important ally.The sculpture has previously been displayed at the Munich Security Conference and the COP30 United Nations climate conference in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025. It was also shown at demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier in 2026 calling for Greenland to be protected from US ambitions.The Strasbourg installation was accompanied by 3D-printed miniature versions of the sculpture, distributed to visitors as “protest tokens”. The artist has said he produced around 20,000 miniatures for distribution to visitors and European Parliament staff.The temporary exhibition in Strasbourg is expected to remain on display until Thursday. Galschiøt plans to exhibit the sculpture again at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, next month. Trump has not publicly commented on the artwork.
Article Summary: Sculpture by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt depicts Trump sitting on the shoulders of a frail, smaller man, with his thighs and sagging belly wrapped around the man's head. Trump holds a golf club in one hand and the scales of justice in the other. The work is also known as the ‘King of Injustice’

Article Title: US suspends 8 tech firms from PERM process: Full list and what it means
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump.

The US administration has suspended eight major technology companies from the employment-based green card process, leaving thousands of foreign professionals, including Indian IT workers, facing uncertainty over their permanent residency plans.The companies named in the October 8 order are Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. The US Department of Labor said it would neither accept new Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) applications involving these firms nor process pending ones.The administration has cited alleged abuse of employment-based immigration programmes and the need to protect American workers. US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of laying off American workers while seeking H-1B approvals and green cards for foreign employees. Cognizant had also faced a suspension of its US green card filings in September amid a probe into possible visa fraud.PERM is a key step in obtaining many employer-sponsored green cards. It requires employers to demonstrate that there are not enough qualified, willing and available American workers for a position and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect wages and working conditions.The suspension does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas or green cards. However, employees with pending PERM applications could face delays, while those whose employers have not yet filed applications may be unable to begin the usual process through these companies. Workers whose PERM certifications have already been approved are in a different position, as the order does not automatically invalidate existing approvals.The decision could create additional uncertainty for H-1B workers approaching the standard six-year limit, particularly those relying on their green card process to qualify for extensions. Some employees may explore sponsorship through another employer, but applications do not automatically transfer when workers change jobs.The duration of the suspension remains uncertain. JD Vance said it would continue “as long as it needs to”. The affected companies could also challenge the decision in federal court. The impact on individual workers will depend on the status of their immigration cases and the length of the suspension.
Article Summary: Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini named. US Department of Labor said it would neither accept new Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) applications involving these firms nor process pending ones.

Article Title: A 21-year-old Tennessee moviegoer noticed an 80-year-old AMC usher emptying trash after a screening and hoped a TikTok fundraiser might bring in $500; strangers donated more than $146,000 in less than
Article Text:
Brooklyn Green spotted an elderly worker emptying rubbish at an AMC theatre in Tennessee and recorded a video of her.

Mary, the 80-year-old cinema worker

Mixed reactions to fundraiser

Mary reacts to fundraiser

A 21-year-old woman in Tennessee, United States raised more than $146,000 in less than 24 hours for an 80-year-old cinema worker after noticing her cleaning up rubbish at an AMC theatre. What began as a TikTok video and a small fundraising effort soon attracted thousands of people online, with donations far exceeding the $500 the young woman had initially hoped to collect.According to WVLT, Brooklyn Green had gone to watch a film with her grandparents at the AMC theatre in Maryville, Tennessee, when she noticed an elderly employee pushing a cleaning cart and emptying rubbish. The woman was working hard, and Green decided to record a short video of her.“I just saw her work ethic. She was just working really hard,” Green told WVLT. She later posted the video on TikTok and created a GoFundMe campaign to help the worker, hoping she could eventually enjoy retirement.Green initially expected that friends and family might contribute around $500. Instead, the video spread rapidly, and donations crossed $100,000 within the first day. The total eventually reached approximately $146,000 before Green returned to the theatre to surprise the woman.After launching the fundraiser, Green returned to the theatre to find the elderly employee. However, the woman was not working that day. Green spoke to a manager and learnt that her name was Mary.According to the report, Mary had worked in theatres for more than 45 years. Managers told Green that she enjoyed her job and did not want to stop working. They said Mary was concerned that things might go downhill for her if she stopped working at her age.Green also learnt that Mary regularly helped other people. According to the information shared with her, Mary supported her church and people experiencing homelessness.Her willingness to help others became another reason Green wanted the fundraising effort to succeed. Green recalled a conversation with Mary about the people she supported.“She told me that she helps a mother and child and some of the homeless, and I told her that it comes back tenfold,” Green said.As the TikTok video gained attention, Green began sharing updates about the fundraising campaign. In one update, she explained that Mary was unaware of the video and the money being collected for her.Green also told followers that Mary might not want to accept the donations. According to the manager, Mary was reluctant to stop working, and Green acknowledged that the elderly woman might choose to give the money to other people or charities.The possibility prompted criticism from some social media users. They questioned whether the donations should be returned if Mary did not want the money or decided against retirement.Green responded by making it clear that Mary would have complete control over the funds. "Guys, I said she will decide regardless what to do with the donations. If she decides to give it to a charity or whatever then that is her decision. She is getting every penny, deep breaths lol," Green wrote.She also acknowledged that some people had criticised her for starting the campaign without first speaking to Mary about retirement. "I have gotten a lot of support, but also a lot of backlash for assuming she wants to retire, as well as her not being aware that I was doing this," Green told Storyful, according to CBS News.Despite the criticism, Green continued with her plan to meet Mary and personally tell her about the donations. Green eventually returned to the AMC theatre while Mary was working and surprised her with news of the fundraising campaign.By then, donations had reached approximately $146,000. Green showed Mary the amount on a tablet, revealing how much money strangers had contributed after watching the TikTok video.Mary was overwhelmed by the response and thanked everyone who had donated.“Thank you so very much to all the wonderful people that have donated money. I’m overwhelmed and certainly blessed by the Lord and you wonderful people,” Mary told WVLT.Following the surprise, Mary asked for the GoFundMe campaign to be paused. She said she had already received more than she could ask for. Meanwhile, Green has decided she will work on other projects intended to support more people.
Article Summary: Brooklyn Green, 21, recorded a video of an elderly worker at an AMC theatre in Tennessee. She posted the video on TikTok and created a GoFundMe campaign to help the worker, hoping she could eventually enjoy retirement. Green initially expected that friends and family might contribute around $500. Instead, the video spread rapidly, and donations crossed $100,000 within the first day.

Article Title: A $132,000 GoFundMe was raised for radio host Ronn Owens; federal review found thousands spent on mortgages, businesses and family transfers
Article Text:
Longtime Bay Area radio legend Ronn Owens. Image Credit: The Mercury News

What happened to the $132,000 Ronn Owens GoFundMe donations

Ronn Owens at the KGO studio. Image Credit: The Jewish News of Northern Carolina

The federal review found most spending went elsewhere

Image Credit: SFist

Why did the bankruptcy case become part of the dispute

The court also examined family transfers and other expenses

What did the judge decide about the bankruptcy

The fundraising questions remain separate from criminal charges

A $132,000 GoFundMe campaign created amid radio host Ronn Owens’ health problems became the focus of a federal review after he and his wife sought bankruptcy protection. Court records examined by the US Trustee showed that only about $17,000 of the money was used for medical and pharmacy expenses, while much larger amounts went towards mortgage payments, contributions to businesses and other spending. The review did not result in criminal charges against Owens or his wife, but it raised concerns about whether donors received what they expected from the campaign.The GoFundMe campaign was launched in January 2025 as Owens faced serious health problems. The longtime KGO radio host had described living with Parkinson’s disease for 23 years, along with four bouts of cancer, including colon cancer, and serious heart issues. The campaign appealed to people familiar with his long broadcasting career and said donations would help Owens and his family through difficult circumstances.According to TheDesk, GoFundMe ultimately paid Owens and his wife, Elizabeth Naylor, $132,480 from the campaign. The US Trustee Program in Phoenix later reviewed more than 18 months of financial records, including the bank account into which the donations were deposited.The examination found that the money was largely spent on expenses unrelated to medical care.The figures examined by the trustee provide the clearest picture of how the money was used. TheDesk reported that around $17,000 went towards medical-related bills, although it was not clear whether all of those expenses were connected specifically to Owens’ cancer treatment. By contrast, $118,898 was identified as spending unrelated to medical needs.More than $61,600 went towards mortgage payments, while nearly $44,400 was recorded as capital contributions to companies owned by Owens. The remaining spending included travel, subscriptions and cash given to a child. SFist also reported that other money went towards credit card bills and transfers to family members.The amounts were significant because the campaign had been presented against the backdrop of Owens’ worsening health and financial difficulties. The trustee’s review looked beyond the original fundraising appeal and followed the money through the couple’s accounts.The GoFundMe spending came under scrutiny during Owens and Naylor’s bankruptcy proceedings. The couple first sought Chapter 13 bankruptcy protection, but later filed under Chapter 11 after the earlier case did not provide the protection they sought. Their bankruptcy proceedings eventually brought their financial records under closer examination.SFist reported that during the period covered by the review, the family had more than $20,000 in monthly income and spent more than $520,000 from its bank accounts. The trustee found that only a relatively small portion of the couple’s financial burden was connected to medical expenses.The US Trustee then argued that the bankruptcy case should be dismissed. TheDesk reported that the trustee’s attorney pointed to the bank and GoFundMe records when assessing the couple’s ability to meet Chapter 11 requirements. The court ultimately agreed that there was no reasonable likelihood of a successful reorganisation.Another part of the financial review concerned money transferred to Owens’ daughter, Laura Owens. RadarOnline reported that financial records showed $19,608 in gifts to her, despite the couple having stated under oath that they had not made gifts worth more than $600 per person during the relevant period.The records also showed spending on consumer credit cards, retail and online purchases and other non-medical expenses. RadarOnline noted that the government did not bring criminal or civil fraud charges against Owens or Naylor, and they were not formally accused of fraud in court.The family transfers received additional attention because Laura Owens had her own legal and financial troubles. RadarOnline reported that she had filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, which was later dismissed, while SFist described her as financially dependent on her parents. Those circumstances formed part of the wider financial background examined during the bankruptcy proceedings.The federal bankruptcy court ultimately dismissed Owens and Naylor’s case and prevented them from filing another bankruptcy action for at least two years. TheDesk reported that Chief US Bankruptcy Judge Madeleine Wanslee cited significant failures to meet Chapter 11 requirements, along with multiple errors and misstatements in the record.The judge also pointed to changes in sworn statements concerning ownership of the home where the couple lived. Naylor agreed to the two-year restriction but disputed the suggestion that the documents and testimony demonstrated wrongdoing. According to TheDesk, she said she was grateful for the donations and had worked with the court in the interest of transparency.The ruling did not determine that the GoFundMe spending itself amounted to criminal wrongdoing. Instead, the judge allowed donors to pursue possible claims against Owens and Naylor in state court. Creditors were also allowed to resume collection efforts.The federal trustee said the financial records raised a serious question about whether GoFundMe donors received what they believed they were supporting. SFist reported that the trustee did not conclude that a law had been broken. The issue of whether the fundraising appeal and subsequent spending created legal claims was left for donors and GoFundMe to pursue outside the bankruptcy case.The campaign itself remained online at the time of SFist’s August 3 report and had raised about $137,000 against a $140,000 goal.
Article Summary: A GoFundMe campaign created amid radio host Ronn Owens’ health problems became the focus of a federal review after he and his wife sought bankruptcy protection. Court records examined by the US Trustee showed that only about $17,000 of the money was used for medical and pharmacy expenses. Much larger amounts went towards mortgage payments, contributions to businesses and other spending. The review did not result in criminal charges against Owens or his wife, but it raised concerns about whether donors received what they expected from the campaign.

Article Title: Isabella Rossellini turned a 27-acre New York farmstead into a protected community farm after conserving 20.8 acres; Mama Farm now runs a member CSA and biodiversity programmes for families and childr
Article Text:
Isabella Rossellini turned a 27-acre New York farmstead into a protected community farm after conserving 20.8 acres (Image Credit: Mama Farm)

From a wooded property to a protected farmstead

Growing food while caring for biodiversity

Mama Farm runs a community-supported agriculture (CSA) programme through which members receive shares of the farm's produce (Image Credit: Mama Farm)

How the community-supported agriculture programme works

Children's activities, workshops and a place to gather

A wooded property on Long Island has become a place where farming, animal care and community activities share the same space. The project is Mama Farm, founded by actress Isabella Rossellini in Brookhaven, New York, in 2013. According to the Peconic Land Trust, Rossellini donated a conservation easement in 2012 that protects 20.8 acres of the property. The farm combines food production with biodiversity initiatives and educational activities for families and children. Its community-supported agriculture programme also connects members with the food grown on the land, making the property a working example of how conservation and community life can go hand in hand.Rossellini established Mama Farm with the idea of bringing agriculture and nature together. The original 27-acre property provided space for growing food while retaining its woodland character. Protecting the land became an important part of the project. The Peconic Land Trust helped conserve 20.8 acres through a conservation easement. This legal arrangement restricts certain forms of development and land use to preserve a property's natural or agricultural value. The land remains privately owned, but the agreement helps protect it from development that could compromise its conservation purpose.The arrangement is particularly relevant on Long Island, where development can put pressure on open spaces and agricultural land. Protecting most of the property helps ensure that farming and nature remain part of its future. Mama Farm's current website describes the property as 28 acres, while earlier accounts refer to the original farmstead as 27 acres. Its activities have also expanded beyond growing food to include animal care, biodiversity and environmental education.At Mama Farm, farming practices are closely connected with its environmental goals. According to the farm's official website, crops are grown from heirloom seeds using organic and regenerative agricultural techniques. Farmer Patty Gentry is associated with its growing operations. The farm says it avoids pesticides, herbicides, insecticides and environmentally harmful fertilisers. These practices reflect its aim of producing food while limiting the potential impact of agriculture on the surrounding environment.Animals are another part of the property. Its sanctuary includes heritage-breed chickens and turkeys, sheep, goats, quail, ducks and other animals. According to Mama Farm, the animals are not slaughtered, although eggs and honey are among the products offered through its community-supported agriculture programme. The use of heirloom seeds and heritage breeds also highlights the importance of agricultural diversity. By keeping traditional varieties and breeds part of a working farm, Mama Farm connects food production with the preservation of older agricultural practices.Mama Farm runs a community-supported agriculture (CSA) programme through which members receive shares of the farm's produce. The model creates a direct connection between the people growing food and those who consume it. Mama Farm offers eggs and honey through its CSA programme, while vegetable shares are arranged with farmer Patty Gentry. The programme connects members with local food production and gives them a closer understanding of where their food comes from.The programme also helps make farming more accessible. Growing food requires planning, attention to the seasons and ongoing care for the land. A CSA gives members a closer view of that process and encourages a relationship with the farm that goes beyond shopping. At Mama Farm, the programme forms part of a wider effort to bring people closer to agriculture while maintaining the property's role as a protected working landscape.Mama Farm's work extends beyond food production. Its activities include workshops, children's programmes, theatre and avant-garde films, offering visitors different ways to explore environmental themes and community life. The farm's website describes its atmosphere as inspired by the Italian piazza, a traditional public square where people gather and exchange ideas. This concept reflects the intention to create a shared space where visitors can spend time together, learn and engage with their surroundings.Children can encounter farm animals and explore the outdoors, while workshops provide opportunities to learn about nature and agriculture. These activities bring environmental themes into the farm's community programmes. The conservation easement provides a foundation for these initiatives by helping protect the land on which they take place.Mama Farm brings together sustainable agriculture, animal care and community participation, showing how protected land can remain productive and accessible. Through the project, Rossellini has linked the preservation of a New York farmstead with practical activities that connect people to food, animals and the natural environment. Its approach demonstrates how conservation can become part of everyday community life while helping safeguard agricultural land for the future.
Article Summary: Isabella Rossellini turned a 27-acre New York farmstead into a protected community farm. The Peconic Land Trust helped conserve 20.8 acres through a conservation easement. The farm combines food production with biodiversity initiatives and educational activities for families and children.

Article Title: Christa Pike makes ‘remarkable’ recovery from 'death' after failed US botched execution
Article Text:
Death row inmate makes progress after surviving two injections during a failed lethal injection

Emotional and psychological impact unclear

Court orders preservation of evidence

Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate who survived a botched lethal injection attempt last week, has made a “profound” recovery and can now walk with assistance and eat, her lawyers said on Thursday.Pike, 50, was left in critical condition after two injections of the execution drug pentobarbital failed to kill her on September 30. Her lawyers said she had also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution.“Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery,” her legal team said in a statement, describing her progress as “remarkable”, BBC reported.However, Pike continues to struggle with the psychological trauma of surviving the failed execution, her lawyers said.“Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die,” they said.Her legal team added that the full emotional and psychological impact of the incident remained unclear and that it was uncertain how long her recovery would take. Despite the ordeal, Pike continued to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim, Colleen Slemmer, they said.Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Slemmer, a 19-year-old schoolmate whom she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed after meeting her at a job training camp for low-income young people.Pike was 18 at the time of the killing, while Shipp was 17. He was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed and remains in prison.Slemmer’s mother, who had supported Pike’s execution, described the failed attempt as a “mess”.The failed execution has raised questions about what went wrong and whether Tennessee could attempt to execute Pike again.On Wednesday, Judge I’Ashea Myles ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the botched procedure, potentially laying the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.Meanwhile, some proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different execution method.
Article Summary: Christa Pike, 50, was left in critical condition after two injections of the execution drug pentobarbital failed to kill her on September 30. Her lawyers said she had also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution. Her legal team added that the full emotional and psychological impact of the incident remained unclear.

Article Title: ‘About 100 H-1B visa holders were on Amazon’s initial team that built AWS’: Ex-employee criticises US green-card suspension for tech firms
Article Text:
Ex-employee shares Amazon’s journey: From makeshift desks to a technology giant

AWS has become a major source of Amazon’s profits

US suspends PERM labour certification for major technology firms

Why H-1B visas are at the centre of the debate

Mathur’s argument about immigrant talent

Shobhit Mathur, co-founder and vice-chancellor of Rishihood University, has defended the contribution of skilled foreign workers to the US technology industry, recalling his experience of joining Amazon on an H-1B visa when the company was still making losses. In a post on X, Mathur said he was part of the initial team that built Amazon Web Services (AWS), adding that approximately 100 H-1B visa holders were involved in Amazon’s early team. His account comes amid renewed debate over skilled immigration after the US administration announced restrictions on green-card sponsorship processing for several technology companies.Mathur recalled that Amazon was operating from a rented building when he joined, with employees working at makeshift desks made from doors inside small cabins. He said the company was making losses at the time and that around 100 H-1B visa holders were part of its initial team. According to Mathur, these professionals contributed their hard work and expertise to building the foundations of Amazon Web Services (AWS), which has since grown into one of the company’s most significant sources of profit.Mathur’s central argument is that foreign professionals can contribute to building businesses that eventually generate substantial economic value.He pointed to AWS as an example, saying that the cloud-computing business has become a major source of Amazon’s profits and helped transform the company’s financial position.Amazon’s published results show the scale of the business Mathur describes. In 2025, AWS generated $128.7 billion in net sales, up 20% from the previous year, and its operating income rose to $45.6 billion from $39.8 billion in 2024. Amazon’s total operating income for the year was $80.0 billion, making AWS responsible for about 57% of it, even though it accounted for roughly 18% of the company’s $716.9 billion in net sales.The share has since climbed past the level Mathur cites. In the second quarter of 2026, AWS sales rose 37% to $42.2 billion and its operating income reached $16.6 billion, or about 60.5% of Amazon’s total operating income.Mathur’s comments come as the Trump administration has intensified scrutiny of employment-based immigration. On October 8, 2026, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspension alongside Vice-President JD Vance. The Department of Labor suspended eight companies from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, known as PERM: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe.PERM is a labour certification process generally required for employment-based green-card applications. Employers typically must demonstrate that there are not sufficient able, willing, qualified and available US workers for the position and that employing a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.The department said it would not accept new PERM applications or process pending ones from the named companies. The reasons differed by company. Sonderling said the six outsourcing firms were suspended outright, while Microsoft and Adobe were suspended due to multiple active federal investigations. Vance singled out Microsoft, saying it laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. Reuters reported that Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, based on Permtrack.app data. TCS said in an exchange filing that it would follow any directions issued by the Department of Labor.The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign professionals for specialty occupations that generally require highly specialised knowledge and a relevant bachelor’s degree or equivalent qualifications. Technology companies use it to recruit software engineers, researchers and other skilled workers from international talent pools.Amazon has been a major participant. One summary of Pew Research Center’s analysis reports that Amazon came first with 11,000 H-1B approvals in 2023. More recently, Amazon’s approvals rose from 9,257 in 2024 to 10,044 in 2025, and a letter from US senators described the FY2025 figure as nearly double that of the next-highest employer. These counts include extensions and transfers, so they do not measure new foreign hires.The programme has also faced criticism over whether some employers use foreign workers to reduce labour costs or replace American employees. The US Department of Labor requires employers hiring H-1B workers to pay at least the higher of the actual wage paid to similarly qualified employees or the prevailing wage for the occupation and location. The department can investigate alleged violations of these requirements.The administration argues that restrictions are necessary to address cases of alleged wage undercutting and displacement. Technology companies and advocates of skilled immigration argue that access to international talent helps businesses recruit specialised workers and develop new products. These competing arguments have made H-1B visas a prominent issue in the wider debate over US technology policy and employment.In his post, Mathur challenged the characterisation of foreign professionals as merely inexpensive labour, arguing that their contributions can extend beyond filling vacancies. He pointed to Amazon's transformation from a loss-making company into a business with a highly profitable cloud-computing division.His closing argument was that companies would struggle to build businesses and wealth without skilled international workers. The post directly connects his early Amazon experience with the current debate over restrictions on foreign-worker immigration.
Article Summary: Shobhit Mathur, co-founder and vice-chancellor of Rishihood University, has defended the contribution of skilled foreign workers to the US technology industry. He recalled his experience of joining Amazon on an H-1B visa when the company was still making losses. Mathur’s central argument is that foreign professionals can contribute to building businesses that eventually generate substantial economic value. He pointed to Amazon Web Services as an example, saying that the cloud-computing business has become a major source of Amazon's profits.

Article Title: America First, powered by foreign talent; five of six tech execs honored by Trump were born outside US
Article Text:
Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives

TOI correspondent from Washington: There was something deliciously awkward and ironic about US President Donald Trump’s celebration of American technological greatness in the White House on Thursday. Of the six technology titans who received the nation’s highest science and tech honours from the MAGA boss, five were born outside the United States. The sole exception was Michael Dell, the Texas-born founder of Dell Technologies.If the MAGA movement’s proposition is that America does not need foreigners to make America great, the White House assembled a plush rebuttal -- complete with medals, billionaires, and a presidential seal of approval. At the ceremony, titled “Science: A New Golden Age,” Trump presented the National Medal of Science to Tesla’s Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Dell received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.The honours recognised extraordinary contributions to computing, semiconductors, artificial intelligence and space exploration.They also offered an inadvertent reminder of a longstanding truth about Silicon Valley and the wider American tech industry: US sci- tech primacy has been built not merely on American ingenuity, but on its ability to attract, educate and retain talent from around the world. That is a slightly inconvenient message for an administration determined to make foreign workers villains in its political narrative.Nobody had a more surreal day on this front than Satya Nadella. In the morning, vice-president JD Vance was unloading on Microsoft, accusing it of abusing employment-based immigration programs while laying off American workers. Vance cited 6,000 US job cuts alongside 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards, announcing that the administration was suspending the company from the program used to sponsor permanent residency for eligible foreign workers. Microsoft disputed the implication that its visa filings represented a wholesale replacement of American employees, saying most were for existing workers.Hours later, there was Nadella in the White House, receiving a presidential medal for helping build one of America’s most consequential technology companies -- from a shambolic administration that managed, in a single working day, to put Microsoft in the immigration penalty box and its chief executive on the national innovation podium. The citation for Nadella praised his “transformative leadership of a critical American technology company, which led to its rejuvenation for a new era of cloud computing,” and his role in building “the hyperscale infrastructure that enabled the training and global deployment of American super intelligence. ”It was a substantial tribute to the Hyderabad-born executive’s transformation of Microsoft into a cloud-computing and artificial-intelligence powerhouse. It was also a reminder that the company’s leadership, like much of the talent sustaining Silicon Valley, does not conform neatly to an America-first immigration script.Vance’s argument is that foreign workers can displace Americans and become vulnerable to employers because their immigration status is tied to their jobs. While tech executives acknowledge that concern deserves scrutiny where companies exploit visa programmes, a blanket hostility to foreign talent is a rather different proposition -- particularly when the administration simultaneously celebrates executives whose achievements have helped make American companies global leaders. “A foreign worker is a problem when applying for a green card but a national treasure when collecting a medal,” one industry insider remarked tartly after the event, asserting that foreign-born tech leaders don’t arrive in the US as geniuses; America is what makes them.Jensen Huang and Lisa Su supplied another irony, this time with a geopolitical edge. Cousins once removed, both were born in Taiwan. Huang has built Nvidia into the dominant force in AI computing, while Su has led AMD’s revival as a formidable competitor in high-performance processors. Their achievements illustrate how Taiwan-born engineering talent has helped shape the technologies on which America’s economic and strategic ambitions increasingly depend.Their recognition comes against the backdrop of Trump’s outreach to Beijing, including his recent high-profile engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Some foreign-policy analysts worry that a transactional approach to relations with China, or concessions made in pursuit of a broader accommodation, could weaken the credibility of America’s commitment to Taiwan’s security. While the medal ceremony did not itself signal any change in US policy towards Taiwan, the juxtaposition was striking: Washington was celebrating two Taiwanese-born executives whose work is central to the global semiconductor industry even as the future of Taiwan remains one of the most consequential questions in US-China relations. Like Nadella, Huang and Su are living illustrations of how global talent reinforce American power. None of that fits comfortably into the MAGA proposition that national greatness can be secured by shutting the door on immigrants.Meanwhile, Sergei Brin and Elon Musk offered another reminder of the complicated origins of American tech success. Brin, born in Moscow in the erstwhile Soviet Union, emigrated to the U.S when he was a child, and went on to co-found Google, helping transform how the world searches for and organises information. Musk, meanwhile, was born in South Africa before moving to America and eventually becoming a US citizen. Through Tesla and SpaceX, he has helped reshape electric vehicles, commercial spaceflight and satellite communications. His relationship with Trump has had its own spectacular ruptures and reconciliations, making his presence at the ceremony -- on a day he has been lashing out at India and its business leadership -- another reminder that the administration’s relationship with tech leaders is rarely short of drama.
Article Summary: Of six tech titans who received the nation’s highest science and tech honours, five were born outside the United States. The sole exception was Michael Dell, the Texas-born founder of Dell Technologies. US sci- tech primacy has been built not merely on American ingenuity, but on its ability to attract, educate and retain talent.

Article Title: In 2004, Shannen Doherty paid $2.56 million for a Malibu home she called her sanctuary; 22 years later, after a $9.5 million posthumous listing and price cut, the property sold for $7.65 million
Article Text:
Photo credit (L-R): AI-generated; Realtor.com

A private refuge in Malibu

Renovated after the Woolsey Fire

Resort-style outdoor space

A difficult sale

Proceeds to go to her mother

The end of a meaningful chapter

Shannen Doherty’s longtime Malibu home has sold for $7.65 million, nearly two years after the actress died following a lengthy battle with cancer. Doherty bought the five-bedroom property for $2.56 million in 2004 and later described it as a private sanctuary where she could escape the demands of Hollywood. The home was listed for $9.5 million in August 2025, more than a year after her death, but attracted a buyer only after several price reductions. Realtor.com reported that the property eventually went under contract after its asking price was reduced to $8.25 million. The final sale closed for $600,000 below that figure, ending the Malibu chapter of a home closely associated with Doherty’s personal life.Doherty purchased the property after establishing herself through major television roles in Beverly Hills, 90210 and Charmed. At the time, she was already familiar with the pressures of public attention, making privacy an important part of the home’s appeal. The actress found that privacy behind mature hedging on one of Malibu’s desirable streets. The estate covers approximately one acre and includes 5,400 square feet of living space. Its location offered a sense of seclusion while still providing the natural beauty and ocean views associated with Malibu.Doherty’s longtime friend Chris Cortazzo, who listed the property and served as executor of her estate, explained to the Wall Street Journal why the home mattered to her. As reported by Realtor.com, Cortazzo said that when someone is a notable figure, a home can become a sanctuary.The property was also a place where Doherty welcomed a small circle of friends. Cortazzo recalled that she hosted regular Italian Nights and Dancing Nights, creating traditions that made the house feel less like a celebrity residence and more like a comfortable gathering place.The property was damaged during the Woolsey Fire in 2018, which affected parts of Malibu and surrounding areas. Doherty later carried out an extensive renovation, rebuilding the home while retaining many of the features that gave it its character, as per the report.It further shared that the exterior combines stucco walls with large sections of glass. Those glass walls open the rear of the residence towards the surrounding landscape and provide expansive views from the main living areas. The primary suite includes a retractable glass wall that strengthens the connection between the bedroom and the outdoors.Inside, the design balances a neutral colour palette with warmer and more personal elements. Beamed ceilings add texture to the living areas, while the kitchen features custom cabinetry and a spacious layout. Sliding barn doors separate the dining room from the den, giving the interiors a rustic detail that contrasts with the home’s modern architecture.Cortazzo also said that the property contained treasures Doherty had collected while travelling. These objects helped make the renovated house feel personal rather than overly staged for the luxury market.The grounds were one of the most important features of the estate. A lap pool with an integrated spa overlooks the ocean and provides a natural centre for the outdoor areas. Privacy hedges surround the property, protecting the gardens and entertaining spaces from public view.The landscaping includes tiered gardens, mature trees and a dining terrace designed for meals outdoors. An edible garden with raised beds and fruit trees adds a practical element to the grounds, giving the property a connection to nature beyond its decorative landscaping.A detached guesthouse sits separately from the main residence. It could be used as a private guest suite, a studio, an extra bedroom or a fitness space. That flexibility increased the property’s appeal for buyers looking for a home that could support both private living and entertaining.The listing described the estate as a combination of California modernism and rustic refinement. It presented the home as a place designed around natural light, indoor-outdoor movement and a calm atmosphere.Doherty’s estate first placed the property on the market for $9.5 million in August 2025. That price was almost four times what she had paid in 2004, although it also reflected the renovation, the land, the views and the size of the residence.The home did not sell immediately. The asking price was reduced several times, eventually reaching $8.25 million in February. Realtor.com later reported that the property had gone pending, although the terms of the offer were not initially disclosed.The final sale price was $7.65 million, which was $600,000 below the last asking price. Compared with Doherty’s original purchase price, the property sold for approximately $5.09 million more, reported Relator.com. The difference does not represent pure profit because it does not account for renovation costs, taxes, maintenance, commissions or other expenses connected with owning and selling the home.Wildfire concerns may also have influenced the pace of the sale. Although the estate was outside the Malibu area affected by the January 2025 California wildfires, buyers had reportedly become more cautious about fire risk. Cortazzo said prospective owners were paying close attention to brush clearance, roofing materials and other safety factors before committing to properties in the region.Because Doherty had no children, proceeds from the sale are expected to go to her mother, Rosa, according to Cortazzo. Doherty was still legally married to photographer Kurt Iswarienko when she died, although the couple had separated in 2023. Their divorce was finalised two days after her death.The sale therefore carried an emotional and practical significance beyond its financial value. It involved the handling of an estate after the death of an actress who had spoken openly about her health, relationships and plans for the future.Doherty was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer in 2015. She later revealed that the cancer had returned and progressed to Stage 4. Through interviews and her Let’s Be Clear podcast, she discussed treatment, fear, hope and her determination to continue living fully.The Malibu home became especially important during those years. It offered a protected space where Doherty could spend time with people close to her and step away from the attention surrounding her illness and career.The sale of Doherty’s Malibu residence closes the story of a house that served as much more than a luxury asset. It was where she created private traditions, rebuilt after a devastating fire and found a measure of calm during an intensely difficult period of her life.For the buyer, the estate offers ocean views, mature landscaping, a lap pool, a guesthouse and a carefully renovated interior. For those who followed Doherty’s career, however, it will remain associated with the actress’s idea of home as a place of protection and connection.Purchased for $2.56 million in 2004, listed for $9.5 million after her death and ultimately sold for $7.65 million, the property has now entered a new chapter. Its next owner will inherit a secluded Malibu estate, while Doherty’s family receives the proceeds from the home she once considered her sanctuary.
Article Summary: Shannen Doherty’s longtime Malibu home has sold for $7.65 million, nearly two years after the actress died following a lengthy battle with cancer. Doherty bought the five-bedroom property for $2.56 million in 2004 and later described it as a private sanctuary where she could escape the demands of Hollywood. The home was listed for $9.5 million in August 2025, more than a year after her death, but attracted a buyer only after several price reductions. The estate covers approximately one acre and includes 5,400 square feet of living space.

Article Title: A Miami airport passenger had an ‘unexplained bulge’; officers found 10 live birds hidden in his underwear
Article Text:
‘Unexplained bulge’ raises suspicion at Miami airport

Six tubes were sewn into his underwear

Eight yellow-faced grassquits and two blue grosbeaks

He said the birds were for “personal use”

A Miami International Airport passenger returning from Cuba was arrested after US Customs and Border Protection officers found 10 live birds concealed in plastic tubes sewn into his underwear. Alberto Hernandez Castillo, 40, a Cuban national and permanent resident of the US, arrived from Havana on October 4 aboard World Atlantic Flight 503 and was selected for a secondary inspection. According to a federal criminal complaint, Castillo declared that he was not bringing animals or wildlife into the US. Officers searching his luggage found no contraband, but then noticed an “unexplained bulge” around his waist and pelvic area. A subsequent pat-down allegedly uncovered six concealed tubes containing the birds.During the secondary inspection, Castillo reportedly told officers that he had travelled to Cuba to visit family and was carrying a carry-on bag and a fanny pack. He signed a Customs Entry Declaration in which he answered “No” when asked whether he was bringing animals or wildlife into the country, according to the complaint.Officers searched his belongings but found nothing unusual.During further questioning, however, they noticed what the complaint described as an “unexplained bulge” at the front of his waist and pelvis. Officers also reported that he appeared nervous. They then took him to a secure area for a pat-down.The pat-down allegedly revealed six clear cylindrical plastic containers wrapped in tape and concealed inside black pockets sewn into Castillo's underwear. The openings of the containers had black mesh attached to allow airflow.Inside the containers were 10 live birds.
